page: Amazon Web Services m8id.24xlarge is a general-purpose, instance-store-equipped cloud server powered by the Nitro hypervisor and Intel Xeon 6975P-C processors. Operating on the x86_64 architecture, this instance features 96 vCPUs across 48 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading, reaching clock speeds of up to 3.9 GHz. It is paired with a massive 480 MB L3 cache, modern instruction sets including AVX-512 and Intel AMX matrix acceleration, and 384 GB of high-frequency DDR5 memory running at 7 GHz, delivering a standard 1:4 core-to-memory ratio.

Hardware bundling includes 5,700 GB of high-speed local NVMe SSD storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 40 Gbps. In benchmark evaluations, the m8id.24xlarge demonstrates exceptional multi-threaded throughput. Multi-core Geekbench testing places it in the top 10% with a score of 22,208, complemented by a top-tier PassMark CPU score of 107,119.74 and top-tier multi-threaded bzip3 decompression at 658.26 GB/sec. Memory read bandwidth reaches 385.12 GB/sec for large blocks, highlighting strong memory subsystem performance alongside high-speed data access.

Tradeoffs emerge primarily in per-thread compute limits. While multi-threaded execution and prompt processing are in the upper deciles, single-core stress-ng performance falls into the middle 50% average range. Similarly, token generation speeds for large language models remain moderate without dedicated GPU acceleration. However, the presence of 5.7 TB of fast local NVMe storage and high-bandwidth DDR5 delivers exceptional qualitative cost efficiency for resource-dense workloads that would otherwise incur elevated secondary EBS or external data transfer overheads.

The m8id.24xlarge is well matched for demanding production deployments requiring balanced compute, heavy memory access, and high local I/O. Optimal workloads include distributed in-memory databases like Redis, massive relational database operations, high-throughput static web serving, enterprise software compilation, and CI/CD pipelines processing large artifact caches.
